list.listitem: Diagnosis of arterial gas embolism is based on clinical history, with support from quantitative electroencephalography (EEG), computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). C
The patient should be given supplemental oxygen in the supine position initially then treated with hyperbaric oxygen as soon as the patient is hemodynamically stable. C
A significant number of patients will experience residual neurologic deficits from cerebral air embolism. C

background.definition: Arterial gas embolism results from the introduction of gas into the pulmonary venous or systemic arterial circulation. This gas can form bubbles which flow into and occlude functional end arteries.

list.listitem: The frequency of venous air embolization following the placement of central venous access is less than 2%; arterial gas embolism is less common in comparison.
The true incidence of cerebral arterial gas embolism is unknown.
In the typical and most severe form, 4% of victims present with cardiac arrest.
Cerebral arterial gas embolism is the major cause of death from diving accidents.
In patients undergoing cardiac surgery or any procedure involving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), an estimated 1% to 3% experience a new stroke.
Air embolism occurs in approximately 0.2% to 0.3% of coronary catheterizations. It is more common among trainees doing percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA).

A systematic review of 19 studies reported a 0.08% rate of symptomatic air embolism following percutaneous transthoracic lung biopsy. Risk factors for air embolism included use of a larger gauge needle (>= 19).
Arterial gas embolism occurs via 3 mechanisms: transpulmonary entry (decompression barotrauma), intracardiac shunt (cardiac septal defect), or direct entry of air into the arterial system.
Decompression barotrauma: rapid termination of an underwarter dive, high-altitude flight, space vehicle excursion, or any other event resulting in a rapid decline in ambient air pressure.

Direct entry: lung injury (pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax), alveolar rupture, or any procedure that involves incision of a vascular bed in the presence of a pressure gradient favoring entry of gas into the vasculature.

Surgical procedures with the highest risk of arterial gas embolization include craniotomy performed in the sitting position, cesarean delivery, liver resection, hip replacement, and any procedure involving ECMO. Using a low pneumoperitoneal pressure during laparascopic liver resection reduced the likelihood of severe air embolism (41% vs 67%, p = 0.003, NNT = 4) in a Chinese randomized trial.
Air embolism has also been reported following diagnostic bronchoscopy, laparascopic cholecystectomy, and ERCP.
As little as 0.05 cc air is enough to cause cerebral ischemia if allowed to enter the cerebral arterial tree.

Decompression barotrauma happens as a diver ascends and the reduction in ambient pressure results in a decrease in partial pressure of various gases in the vasculature. This reduction in partial pressure allows gas to come out of solution and form bubbles according to Boyle's law, resulting in emboli.

Gas bubbles migrate into small arteries—on average 30 to 60 micrometers in diameter—resulting in reduced distal perfusion and subsequent ischemia. An inflammatory response to the gas bubbles also results in cellular damage and cerebral edema from capillary leak.

Smaller bubbles that do not occlude vessels may still cause transient cerebral or coronary ischemia, endothelial damage, and activation of an inflammatory response, which can still cause secondary ischemia.
Distribution of small gas bubbles into the skeletal muscles or viscera are usually well tolerated without significant residual effects.
Distribution of gas bubbles into the coronary or cerebral arteries can be fatal because of the sensitivity of these tissues to even short periods of decreased perfusion and hypoxia.
Cardiac surgery and any procedure involving ECMO can result in periods of cerebral hypoperfusion, as well as the risk of arterial gas embolism.
Hemodynamic complications of air embolism include decreased mean arterial pressure, decreased cardiac output, increased pulmonary artery resistance and pressure, and myocardial ischemia.
Pulmonary complications of air embolism include hypoxia, hypercarbia, pulmonary edema, and bronchoconstriction.
Ischemic end-organ damage may affect the brain, spinal cord, heart, and skin.
Diagnosis of arterial gas embolism is based primarily on clinical history, particularly in patients who display signs of symptoms intraoperatively or perioperatively. C

Brain CT is the best initial modality for the evaluation of cerebral arterial gas embolism to demonstrate focal ischemia. CT should be followed by diffusion-weighted brain MRI to assess the extent of cerebral injury. C
Quantitative EEG can detect evidence of cerebral arterial gas embolism and can be used to determine improvement during hyperbaric oxygen therapy. C
Coronary arterial gas embolism is suggested by clinical and electrocardiography (ECG) findings that indicate myocardial ischemia or infarction. C

Consider air embolism in the patient who has had a procedure or an event associated with the condition, such as a cardiac, pulmonary, otolaryngolic, or neurosurgical procedure; barotrauma; central venous catheter placement; or penetrating chest trauma.

The most severe and classic presentation is loss of consciousness and cardiac arrest, seen in 4% of patients. Any cardiac or focal neurologic symptoms in the correct context can indicate a coronary or cerebral arterial gas embolic event, respectively. Diagnosis in postoperative patients can be complicated by residual effects of anesthesia or adverse responses to anesthesia, which can resemble the effects of cerebral arterial gas embolization.

Symptoms of arterial gas embolism include dyspnea, sudden inspiration or "gasp reflex," dizziness or lightheadedness, chest pain, and an "impending sense of doom." Physical findings may include wheezing, rales, tachypnea, or respiratory failure; altered mental status or new neurologic deficit; tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distention, or shock; livedo reticularis; or retinal artery bubbles.

The most common manifestation of cerebral arterial gas embolism is a sudden change in sensorium. Cerebral arterial gas embolism can manifest as the sudden development of focal neurologic symptoms or global neurologic dysfunction. In one study, the initial neurologic manifestations of a cerebral air embolism included impaired consciousness (70%), focal motor deficits (60%), seizures (11%), visual disturbances (10%), dysarthria or aphasia (5%), and vertigo (5%).

Impairment of respiratory of circulatory function as a consequence of cerebral arterial gas embolism can manifest as decreased respiratory rate, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, circulatory failure, and cardiac arrhythmias or arrest. In one study involving both venous and arterial cerebral air emboli, 26% of patients manifested hemodynamic disturbances and 23% had respiratory disturbances, with 51% requiring mechanical ventilation.
In postoperative patients, impaired consciousness or difficulty recovering from anesthesia can be the presenting symptom of cerebral arterial gas embolism.

Coronary arterial gas embolism can manifest similarly to a typical thromboembolic myocardial infarction, characterized by typical ECG changes (ST elevation or depression, T wave inversions), arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest.
When air embolism is clinically suspected, order arterial blood gases and chest x-ray.
Plain radiographs, which can visualize large amounts of intravascular air, CT, and transcranial Doppler are the recommended studies to diagnose cerebral arterial gas embolism.

In some cases, cerebral arterial gas embolism can be distinguished from cerebral infarct or hemorrhage on CT, although the changes seen with arterial gas embolism are subtle and typically not well visualized. The typical findings on CT scan include pneumocephalus and cerebral edema, which may be seen with or without arterial infarction. Air may sometimes also be seen in the subarachnoid spaces.

CT may not be effective if not performed immediately after the embolic event because air is quickly resorbed from the vasculature into tissues. Therefore, a brain CT should be performed as soon as cerebral arterial gas embolism is suspected.

After a diagnosis of cerebral arterial gas embolism is suggested by CT, an MRI should be performed to evaluate the extent of cerebral injury. Diffusion-weighted MRI may not show signs of ischemia if performed immediately after the event, but findings of multiple restricted diffusion areas in a gyriform pattern, or in watershed areas with decompression barotrauma, have been associated with cerebral arterial gas embolism.
Gas bubbles can sometimes be detected on retinal examination, but their absence does not rule-out cerebral arterial gas embolism.

Hemoconcentration, suggested by an elevated hematocrit level, may sometimes be seen in cases of arterial gas embolism, possibly due to extravascular shifts of fluids into injured tissues. This is, however, a nonspecific finding.

In a pig model, quantitative EEG (qEEG) was able to demonstrate changes in brain function after cerebral arterial gas embolism and was used to monitor recovery after appropriate treatment. The investigators believed that EEG may be used to measure treatment outcomes but did not comment on the applicability of qEEG to initial diagnosis and evaluation.
Echocardiogram may reveal air in right ventricle; one may also see right ventricular dilation from pulmonary artery hypertension.
ECG may reveal tachycardia, peaked P waves, ST segment, or T wave changes, and other signs of acute myocardial infarction.

Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical suspicion and patient history, particularly if neurologic or cardiac symptoms present shortly after a patient undergoes a rapid change in ambient pressure or an invasive surgical procedure.

Large volume air emboli may cause cardiovascular collapse; end-organ ischemia, including brain and spinal cord; or even death. A severe air embolus may mimic a cardiovascular accident, acute myocardial infarction, or even a pulmonary thromboemboli.
Tests that can support the diagnosis of cerebral arterial gas embolism include EEG, CT, and MRI.
ECG changes typical of ischemia or infarction can support the diagnosis of coronary arterial gas embolism.
Initial management involves stabilization of the patient, cardiopulmonary support as needed, and then initiation of the diagnostic work-up.
The primary goals of treatment are to stabilize the patient, prevent further air embolization, initiate supportive care, and restore pre-embolus physiology. C
The patient should initially be given maximum supplemental oxygen and placed in the supine position. The Trendelenburg position should be avoided as this can aggravate cerebral edema. C
Hyperbaric oxygen is the treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism and treatment should be initiated as soon as possible. C
The use of infusion, anticoagulants, corticosteroids, and lidocaine are controversial therapies for cerebral arterial gas embolism and are currently not officially recommended. C

The use of anticoagulant therapy is currently not recommended, though there is some evidence that heparin may be beneficial. The counterargument is the possibility of hemorrhagic conversion in already infarcted tissue.

The use of corticosteroids to reduce brain edema is also controversial. Arterial air embolism results in cytotoxic brain edema, which usually does not respond to corticosteroids and may in fact be aggravated by steroid use.

Lidocaine therapy has been proposed as a treatment for cerebral arterial gas embolism. However, a recent study showed no neuroprotective effects of lidocaine, including no differences in self-rating of memory function or length of intensive care unit or hospital stay.
Stabilize the patient and attempt to prevent further embolization and identify the cause.
Supplemental oxygen at the highest available concentrations should be administered to treat hypoxia and hypoxemia caused by the arterial gas embolus.

Place the patient in the supine position, avoiding the Trendelenburg position as this can worsen cerebral edema. The gas bubble's buoyancy cannot counteract the force of blood flow toward the brain, even in the Trendelenburg position, so it is not useful to place the patient in this position.
In patients undergoing laparoscopic liver resection, low pneumoperitoneal pressure (10 mm vs 15 mm) reduced the risk of gas embolism ((41% vs 67%, p = 0.003, NNT = 4).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the first-line treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of gas bubbles in the vasculature and increases the amount of oxygen dissolved in blood plasma, thereby improving oxygen diffusion into tissues.

Initiation of hyperbaric oxygen to patients within 3 hours of cerebral arterial gas embolism was shown in a small study to significantly improve neurologic recovery, as compared with those whose treatment was delayed between 9 and 20 hours.
Although studies have stressed the importance of initiating hyperbaric oxygen therapy early, these same studies have not produced enough data to determine recommendations for duration of treatment.

There is some evidence that gas embolism can lead to hemoconcentration from extravasation of gases into tissues, which can lead to increased blood viscosity when there is already decreased microvascular circulation. Therefore, some experts advocate hemodilution to a hematocrit level of 30%.

Some experts advocate the use of colloid over crystalloid solutions because of the possibility of crystalloid worsening cerebral edema. Additionally, as the goal is normovolemia, it is recommended that central venous pressure should be maintained at 12 mm Hg and urine output at 1 to 2 mL per kg per hour.

Seizures resulting from cerebral arterial gas embolism should be treated with barbiturates if they do not respond to benzodiazepines. Barbiturates have been shown to decrease cerebral oxygen consumption, intracranial pressure, free radical production, and the release of catecholamines.

Hepatic portal venous gas can be caused by a variety of gastrointestinal conditions including most commonly intestinal ischemia, intestinal perforation or fistula, intestinal obstruction, abdominal infection including appendicitis, and acute hemorrhage or necrotizing pancreatitis. It is generally considered to be a surgical emergency,
Significant neurocognitive deficits remain in 30% to 65% of patients who experience intraoperative stroke. These deficits may remain at least 5 years in 42% of these patients.B

In one study of a small number of patients with cerebral arterial gas embolism, approximately 39% of patients had a good outcome with total neurologic recovery, and 61% had a poor outcome including lasting neurologic deficits and death. A shorter period before initiation of hyperbaric oxygen therapy correlated with a better outcome.B
